item.title: My Windows 11 PC can run containers without Docker Desktop, and the entire setup took one command
item.itunes:title: My Windows 11 PC can run containers without Docker Desktop, and the entire setup took one command
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It has been a little more than a month since WSL 3.0.1 came out, and it's already changing the way I run my Linux containers. One of the most distinctive features that interested me is the fact that it adds the wslc command that can pull images, run containers, map ports, and even build images from a Containerfile straight from PowerShell or CMD.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

What's funny is that Microsoft itself used to recommend using Docker Desktop in its WSL container tutorial in the past, but has now taken to teaching wslc on the same Microsoft Learn page. Following those instructions, I set it up on my main PC with a Ryzen 5 7600X and an RTX 4070 Ti Super. To my absolute delight, I had my first container running in under a minute after starting the update, and now I'm convinced there's no simpler way to run containers if you're on Windows 11. Here's why, and how it's done.

The whole installation process is one command

Type in wsl --update, and you're nearly done

The setup is remarkably easy and possibly as straightforward as it gets. If you follow Microsoft's official guidance, the setup will begin and end in PowerShell. The first thing you'd want to do is check if you already have WSL version 3.0.1 or later through wsl --version, which is possible if you've updated it recently. If not, wsl --update pulls the latest release, and that one command is the entire installation process.

If your PC doesn't have WSL or if it's a fresh Windows 11 install, you'll have to use wsl --install to set it up first. Everything that happens after is just post-setup verification. You can run wslc version to confirm the new command is live, and thereafter run wslc run --rm hello-world to pull a small test image and print a greeting from inside the Linux container. Believe it or not, that's literally it.

On my PC, the first container printed the greeting in less than 10 seconds after I hit Enter, and that's including the image download. Absolutely nowhere was I asked to sign in, reboot my PC, or accept some license, which is as smooth as containerization has ever been on Windows 11.

WSL containers are about to make Docker on Windows obsolete

You don't need Docker anymore on Windows

9
By  Anurag Singh

My RTX 4070 Ti Super works inside the container like a dream

The Windows driver I already had did all the work

My workflow involves working a lot with local LLMs through llama.cpp, and llama.cpp publishes official CUDA container images. The catch is that an inference server in a container is worth running only if it can reach the GPU, because without it, the inference falls back to the CPU, and on a 7600X processor, that turns a quick response from the model into something you'd have to wait three business days to finish. Obviously, that's not the experience anyone into local AI inference wants.

The good news about it all is that WSL has been handing Nvidia GPUs to Linux for years through the same driver Windows already uses, so there's no additional Linux driver I have to hunt down. If you've ever used Docker like I have, you'll already know how to point it to your GPU, because wslc accepts the same --gpus all flag. To make sure it was working as expected, I ran Nvidia's small CUDA base image with: 

wslc run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.9.1-base-ubuntu24.04 nvidia-smi 

Sure enough, it confirmed that the container saw my RTX 4070 Ti Super with its 16GB of VRAM and driver version 617.14, which is the same version Windows 11 reports. On a regular Linux machine, this would involve installing Nvidia's Container Toolkit and configuring Docker to use it. Here, I never had to install anything.

When I confirmed that it works, the only thing left to confirm was how well it works. I pointed llama.cpp's official CUDA image at my Gemma 4 E4B model file that I use on Windows, mounted directly from my models folder. Both runs used the same Q4_K_M quantization with full GPU offload at 128K context, with the same prompt, and a 256-token reply. Native llama.cpp generated between 128 and 132 tokens/second across two runs, whereas the container produced 124 tokens/second both times. Suffice it to say, that's a gap I'll never notice.

Microsoft is baking Linux containers into Windows, and it might end my reliance on Docker Desktop

Linux containerization is now a default feature

5
By  Ty Sherback

WLSC doesn't replace Docker Desktop for me, and it doesn't have to

Compose is missing, and Microsoft's working on it

I'm not going to talk about how wslc is better than Docker Desktop, or if I prefer one over another, especially not at this time, when compose is clearly missing from the picture. Since wslc is still relatively new, it's missing a built-in compose runtime and, as such, a comparison like that wouldn't be fair.

It helps to know that Microsoft has already acknowledged compose as the most requested wslc feature and said that it's what the team is working on next, with the goal of running existing compose files without changes. Besides that, Docker Desktop also has a couple of other things going for it. It can switch to Windows containers while wslc only runs Linux ones. It's also free for users like myself, and the paid plans are only required for larger organizations.

It has never been easier to launch a Linux container

For single containers, GPU workloads, and tests in a jiffy, wslc offers a path to spin up Linux containers in a second, and that's something many users like myself have come to appreciate. If you don't rely on compose, you can't go wrong with either of the two.

It is worth knowing though that setting up Linux containers is a lot easier and wslc takes a lot of the initial friction out of the loop. If you need compose today but would rather skip Docker Desktop, Podman Desktop and Rancher Desktop are other free, open-source alternatives that handle compose files on top of WSL.

Windows Subsystem for Linux


Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) lets you run Linux tools and applications directly on Windows without dual-booting. This is Microsoft’s repository for its source code, issue reports, and contributions.

item.title: My favorite alternative to Notion isn't Obsidian or OneNote, it's something that works offline and still syncs everywhere
item.itunes:title: My favorite alternative to Notion isn't Obsidian or OneNote, it's something that works offline and still syncs everywhere
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Notion is often the first app that comes to mind for managing notes, projects, and everyday work. But it's not the only option worth considering. I've been looking for a tool that gives me more freedom over how I work without adding unnecessary complexity. Obsidian and OneNote are popular choices, but I found another app that deserves more attention. Anytype takes a different approach to productivity, and some of its features make it a compelling alternative to Notion. Here's why it caught my attention and why it's worth trying.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Anytype gives me the offline-first workspace I wanted

A productivity app that works offline

The biggest reason I liked Anytype was that I could use it without an internet connection. I didn't want an app that became useless whenever my Wi-Fi stopped working. I wanted something I could rely on, even when I was offline.

Anytype stores my data on my device instead of depending entirely on the cloud. This means I can open my existing notes, read them, and continue working without an internet connection. I don't have to worry about losing access to my workspace just because I'm traveling or dealing with a network issue.

What I liked most was that I didn't have to sacrifice a good user experience to get this freedom. Anytype has a clean interface and feels like a modern productivity app, rather than a basic text editor. It gives me a comfortable place to work without making an internet connection a requirement for everyday tasks.

My changes sync across devices

Without making the cloud the center of everything

With Anytype, I don't have to stick to one device to get my work done. I can use it on my desktop when I'm writing and switch to my phone to check something or capture a quick idea. Having my workspace available across devices makes my daily workflow much easier.

What I like is how this works with its local-first approach. My data stays on my device, while Anytype offers ways to sync it with my other devices. I don't have to depend on a traditional cloud-based workspace to keep everything connected.

Of course, syncing changes between devices still requires a connection at some point. When I'm offline, I can keep working locally, and my changes sync when connectivity returns. This gives me more flexibility without making internet access a constant requirement.

I also don't have to keep sending files to myself or manually copying notes between devices. I can focus on my work and let Anytype handle the syncing in the background. For me, that balance between local access and cross-device convenience is what makes it stand out.

I turned Obsidian into a personal command center with these 6 free plugins

Obsidian can be much more than a second brain, and these plugins prove it.

1
By  Yash Patel

Organizing information in Anytype takes a different approach

A fresh take on organizing information

It took me a little time to understand how Anytype organizes information, but I started to like it once I got used to it. Instead of treating everything as a separate note or page, it uses objects to represent different types of information. An object can be a simple note, a task, a person, or a project.

I found this approach useful because I could organize information based on how it relates to other things. For example, I could keep my blog ideas and research notes connected to a project instead of leaving them scattered across different pages. This made it easier to find related information when I needed it.

Anytype also offers sets and collections to help organize these objects. I could group related information and build a structure that suited my workflow. It felt more flexible than simply creating folders and subfolders for everything.

It offers more than a place to store my notes

It does much more than I expected

Beyond the basics, Anytype has several features that make it useful for everyday work. I can create documents using its block editor, which supports text, headings, lists, images, videos, files, links, and tables. This gives me enough flexibility to create anything from a simple checklist to a detailed research document.

I also like the built-in database views. I can display information as a table, gallery, or Kanban board, depending on what I'm working on. The Kanban view is particularly useful for tracking tasks through different stages. Templates are another helpful addition because they save me from creating the same layouts repeatedly.

Anytype also supports bookmarks, file attachments, and a graph view that helps me explore connections across my knowledge base. I can customize my workspace with widgets to keep important sections within easy reach. If I want to work with someone else, its collaboration features include chats and sharing content.

These features make Anytype more than a simple note-taking app. It gives me several tools for writing, planning, and managing information without needing a separate app for every task.

My favorite self-hosted Notion alternatives after testing dozens of different options.

By  Yash Patel

I finally found a workspace that works on my terms

Anytype may not replace every feature of Notion, but it comes close to what I want from a productivity app. I like having control over my workspace without being tied to a single way of working. There is a learning curve, and it may not suit everyone, but I think it's worth trying if you value flexibility and privacy. For me, it's a refreshing change from the usual alternatives.

In the pursuit of preserving these games (and to possibly cash the nostalgia cheque), developers try to make them accessible on marketplaces like Steam, Xbox, and the PlayStation Store by developing "remasters", but the problem is that, in doing so, it often happens that they end up changing the very things that made the originals so great in the first place.

There's always going to be exceptions to this, but three releases from the past decade have made me hesitant to reach for a remaster when the original, lightly upscaled, still does the job better. Here are three such examples that might just make you skeptical about remasters, too.

Konami's HD Collection turned Silent Hill 3 into a parody of itself

The scariest thing was how the game world was "reimagined"

Silent Hill 3 is one of the games from the PS2 era that I'll take any excuse to go back to, and one of the reasons why every PC I own has a PCSX2 emulator installed. It is also one of the reasons why I've never felt the need to play Konami's HD Collection, even though it can often be found at a discount on the Xbox Store, ready and optimized for my Xbox Series X.

The list of reasons why not is quite long, although I bet if you were to ask a fan of the original games, the reasons would be quite similar. If you ponder hard about what imparted the eeriness to the original atmosphere of the game environment, chances are, the characteristic fog would be on the list of the top three reasons. It was an integral aspect of the setting and the ambiance, and it also happens to be one of the things that the HD Collection completely butchered. I'd even argue that the fog is to Silent Hill what Master Chief is to Halo, and cars are to Forza.

The rest of the port had its own problems, from re-recorded voice acting to re-introduced bugs the original team had already fixed. All of those issues tell me that the best way to revisit the games may just be to take the old PS2 disc off the shelf, get the latest build of PCSX2, and let the emulator take care of the rest.

4 modern games that failed to out-shine their retro originals

Having more money and better technology available did nothing for these games

4
By  David Carcasole

Rockstar's Definitive Edition shrank the San Andreas I grew up with

This Grove Street isn't home, but at least it was before Rockstar...

GTA San Andreas was the game that taught me what an open world was supposed to feel like. The last time I spent any real time with the game was through the Definitive Edition as I tested the leaked DLSS 5 build, and I wrote positively about it. What I didn't say there, because it took me another week of playing to notice, was that DLSS 5 was doing the job Rockstar should have shipped the Definitive Edition with.

If I just turned off the neural rendering layer, I'd get a glimpse of the remaster that sits underneath, which launched in 2021 to one of the worst receptions a Rockstar game has had. The character models looked funny if not grotesque, poorly proportioned, and a caricature of the originals.

With the original, Rockstar built a world that you could lose yourself in, and one of the most defining aspects of that world was the radio. If you don't believe me, you can visit Tom Petty's Runnin' Down a Dream on YouTube and find at least four top comments stating, "GTA San Andreas brought me here."

And so, one of the most unforgivable problems, though, was the fact that the game had missing content. A lot of the songs defined certain moments in the game, be it driving from Los Santos to San Fierro, running from the police in a hot pursuit, or just casually exploring the countryside. About 16 licensed tracks didn't make their way from the original game to the remaster. That really isn't something my DLSS 5 layer can fix.

This made me question. For someone who is looking for a nostalgia trip back to San Andreas, does the Definitive Edition provide the best way for it? Considering all the aspects that I mentioned, it certainly isn't providing the complete experience. The version that does offer the complete experience, however, happens to be the one Rockstar pulled off Steam the week the remaster hit the marketplace.

Capcom's Resident Evil 3 is a guided tour of what the original was

Is it really much of a remake when most of it wasn't remade?

On the subject of beloved content from the game that never made it to the remasters, the Resident Evil 3 Remake is something that cannot be left out of the conversation. It hurts to see it affect one of the most distinctive and visually important aspects of the game, and RE3's case makes it painfully clear. Saint Michael's Clock Tower was cut as a playable location, the Raccoon Park was reduced to a short connector area with no content, and the Dead Factory as well as the Grave Digger boss were completely absent.

If you want to get a sense of just how badly this landed with the fans, all you have to do is search for "Resident Evil 3 Remake" on YouTube and watch the first few results come up with walkthroughs for installing a mod that restores the cut content. Of course, that's one way to get that content back, but if you don't have a proclivity towards modding, the GOG re-release of the 1999 offers a rather frictionless way to experience Raccoon City the way it was first envisioned.

10 games that were so bad they killed their franchises

A lot of game franchises have bad releases, but these 10 sunk their entire franchise all together

15
By  Dylan Turck

Upscaling respects the original; remasters rarely do

There's a fine balance between optimizing a game to meet the visual polish that modern players expect versus deconstructing and reconstructing it altogether to suit modern audiences and their gameplay habits. Clearly, one of those approaches turns the game into a different product, while the other just enhances the original vision. Until developers learn the difference, I'm happy to just reach for the original disk.

item.itunes:title: My local models are worse than Claude at almost everything, but they still run most of my workflow for $0
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's not lost on me that any one of Anthropic's models can outperform the models I run on my 16GB Nvidia GPU. I'd wager even Sonnet 5.5 can write much better code, keep track of conversations that just go on and on, and catch mistakes that both my Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4 would walk right past. If you put them side by side on any benchmark, Claude will take the win in literally any workflow, and it won't be close.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

And yet, when I look back on a typical week, my local AI stack running on my RTX 4070 Ti Super gets more prompts from me than Claude ever does. It's not because I'm an advocate for self-hosting or have any clever tweaks that make my local models work better, but because some of what I ask simply involves data I'd rather not upload, some of it is code that doesn't need a frontier model on the first attempt, and the remainder are tasks too trivial to spend my cloud tokens on.

Here's why I'm relying more on the models that run on my PC than on Anthropic's servers, and why I think it's the better approach, both fiscally and logically.

My local models offer me complete privacy

I'm not losing any sleep giving my financial data to Gemma 4 E4B

Once every month, my bank's app generates a spending report that can be exported to a PDF. It gives me an insight into the many ways I've splurged, which is descriptive, but not quite informative in the way I'd like it to be.

Often I'd find myself thinking just how convenient it would be if there was some way to query these documents and ask a model that has all of this context to see if any of this data could be turned into actionable information that I can use to hit the savings target I set at the start of the year, which category is eating into the biggest share and which months I overshoot without noticing. All of these questions warrant a conversation, and a bar graph and a flow chart can't give me that.

I'm also cautious enough to not just drag and drop all of that data onto a Claude chat, so instead, I drag and drop it into a session with Gemma 4 E4B. Since this variant has vision capabilities and supports up to 128K context, it's perfectly suited to the job of parsing a dozen PDFs in a single setting and holding the thread across a conversation that can take up an entire afternoon. Since I'm only looking for answers to simple one-liner questions that don't involve deep reasoning, it doesn't really matter if it can't draw up interactive visuals of my month-on-month expenditure, and does the job just fine.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

18
By  Abhinav Raj

Not all of my code needs a frontier model to fix

I save all my cloud tokens for the biggest blunders, and everything else goes to Qwen3:30B

I've previously talked about how Claude on any tier can feel strangely restrictive when it comes to iterative coding sessions, unless you're a part of the highest paid Max or Enterprise tiers. For a customer like myself on a Claude Pro plan, there are many kinds of usage limits in place that can potentially break a workflow, like the dreaded 5-hour rolling session limit, the weekly limit, or the shared pool cap that applies at busy hours.

These feel like setbacks when I'm in the middle of a long session. Of course, when the limits kick in, anyone would argue that it's time to switch to a local model and keep going, but that comes with its own task-switching cost. All the context needs to be moved from A to B, and that is a problem since that very movement can break the trail of reasoning that got the session this far.

That's why I found it prudent to flip the order instead. I find that when my Qwen3:30B MoE model gets the first pass at the coding, it greatly reduces my token usage on Claude, which can be reserved for the final finishing touches of whatever Python app that I'm working on.

There's also a cost benefit to it, since in an experiment I ran a few weeks ago on a Pygame project, I found that handing Claude Code a working build from Qwen3:30B and asking it to refine it from there only cost $0.77, while asking it to build the same Pygame from scratch cost $1.35, amounting to a cost reduction of 43%.

I replaced my $20 ChatGPT and Claude subscriptions with local AI to cut costs, but it backfired

Free AI models looked like a bargain until I factored in the real cost.

3
By  Yash Patel

Claude's limits are too prohibitive for trivia

Gemma 4 does a fine job recommending games to play or shows to watch anyway

Not everything I use an AI model for relates to work, and anything that isn't strictly for work can't justify the expenditure of the expensive cloud usage credits or tokens on. Obviously, that's because it is eating into my weekly usage limits, and I don't want them to act as a stopper in the middle of a project that disrupts the entire chain of ideation and refinement.

But that doesn't mean I can't get my fix of recommendation lists from an AI model altogether. For the kind of queries that fall in the trivia bucket, like what game I should play next, which show would fill the void that got created by the last one I finished, which book would suit the mood I am in, Gemma 4 handles just as well. I've previously tested this capability in action, wherein I had the model recommend games against Steam's Interactive Recommender, and Gemma 4 gave me better recommendations than the store that sold me all my games in the first place.

I replaced the expensive Claude Pro subscription with these local models, and my productivity didn’t drop a bit

Local-first vibe coding

23
By  Parth Shah

Claude may be the best, but my local AI stack does more for me

There's nothing defeating Claude and its various models in the AI service industry today when it comes to deep reasoning, zero-shot coding, debugging, or perhaps even research. It's clearly the superior service. But for many day-to-day tasks, you simply don't require frontier reasoning capabilities, and that's precisely where I reach for my local AI stack that costs me $0 to run.

I'd wager even Sonnet 5.5 can write much better code, keep track of conversations that just go on and on, and catch mistakes that both my Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4 would walk right past. If you put them side by side on any benchmark, Claude will take the win in literally any workflow, and it won't be close.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

And yet, when I look back on a typical week, my local AI stack running on my RTX 4070 Ti Super gets more prompts from me than Claude ever does. It's not because I'm an advocate for self-hosting or have any clever tweaks that make my local models work better, but because some of what I ask simply involves data I'd rather not upload, some of it is code that doesn't need a frontier model on the first attempt, and the remainder are tasks too trivial to spend my cloud tokens on.

Here's why I'm relying more on the models that run on my PC than on Anthropic's servers, and why I think it's the better approach, both fiscally and logically.

My local models offer me complete privacy

I'm not losing any sleep giving my financial data to Gemma 4 E4B

Once every month, my bank's app generates a spending report that can be exported to a PDF. It gives me an insight into the many ways I've splurged, which is descriptive, but not quite informative in the way I'd like it to be.

Often I'd find myself thinking just how convenient it would be if there was some way to query these documents and ask a model that has all of this context to see if any of this data could be turned into actionable information that I can use to hit the savings target I set at the start of the year, which category is eating into the biggest share and which months I overshoot without noticing. All of these questions warrant a conversation, and a bar graph and a flow chart can't give me that.

I'm also cautious enough to not just drag and drop all of that data onto a Claude chat, so instead, I drag and drop it into a session with Gemma 4 E4B. Since this variant has vision capabilities and supports up to 128K context, it's perfectly suited to the job of parsing a dozen PDFs in a single setting and holding the thread across a conversation that can take up an entire afternoon. Since I'm only looking for answers to simple one-liner questions that don't involve deep reasoning, it doesn't really matter if it can't draw up interactive visuals of my month-on-month expenditure, and does the job just fine.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

18
By  Abhinav Raj

Not all of my code needs a frontier model to fix

I save all my cloud tokens for the biggest blunders, and everything else goes to Qwen3:30B

I've previously talked about how Claude on any tier can feel strangely restrictive when it comes to iterative coding sessions, unless you're a part of the highest paid Max or Enterprise tiers. For a customer like myself on a Claude Pro plan, there are many kinds of usage limits in place that can potentially break a workflow, like the dreaded 5-hour rolling session limit, the weekly limit, or the shared pool cap that applies at busy hours.

These feel like setbacks when I'm in the middle of a long session. Of course, when the limits kick in, anyone would argue that it's time to switch to a local model and keep going, but that comes with its own task-switching cost. All the context needs to be moved from A to B, and that is a problem since that very movement can break the trail of reasoning that got the session this far.

That's why I found it prudent to flip the order instead. I find that when my Qwen3:30B MoE model gets the first pass at the coding, it greatly reduces my token usage on Claude, which can be reserved for the final finishing touches of whatever Python app that I'm working on.

There's also a cost benefit to it, since in an experiment I ran a few weeks ago on a Pygame project, I found that handing Claude Code a working build from Qwen3:30B and asking it to refine it from there only cost $0.77, while asking it to build the same Pygame from scratch cost $1.35, amounting to a cost reduction of 43%.

I replaced my $20 ChatGPT and Claude subscriptions with local AI to cut costs, but it backfired

Free AI models looked like a bargain until I factored in the real cost.

3
By  Yash Patel

Claude's limits are too prohibitive for trivia

Gemma 4 does a fine job recommending games to play or shows to watch anyway

Not everything I use an AI model for relates to work, and anything that isn't strictly for work can't justify the expenditure of the expensive cloud usage credits or tokens on. Obviously, that's because it is eating into my weekly usage limits, and I don't want them to act as a stopper in the middle of a project that disrupts the entire chain of ideation and refinement.

But that doesn't mean I can't get my fix of recommendation lists from an AI model altogether. For the kind of queries that fall in the trivia bucket, like what game I should play next, which show would fill the void that got created by the last one I finished, which book would suit the mood I am in, Gemma 4 handles just as well. I've previously tested this capability in action, wherein I had the model recommend games against Steam's Interactive Recommender, and Gemma 4 gave me better recommendations than the store that sold me all my games in the first place.

I replaced the expensive Claude Pro subscription with these local models, and my productivity didn’t drop a bit

Local-first vibe coding

23

Claude may be the best, but my local AI stack does more for me

There's nothing defeating Claude and its various models in the AI service industry today when it comes to deep reasoning, zero-shot coding, debugging, or perhaps even research. It's clearly the superior service. But for many day-to-day tasks, you simply don't require frontier reasoning capabilities, and that's precisely where I reach for my local AI stack that costs me $0 to run.

item.title: My NAS sits idle 95% of the time, so I moved my desktop's chores onto it
item.itunes:title: My NAS sits idle 95% of the time, so I moved my desktop's chores onto it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The reality of owning a heavy desktop workstation is that it draws massive amounts of power at idle, runs loud fans for minor background tasks, and sits dormant or off for large portions of the day. However, your home storage server or NAS will probably sit plugged in 24/7, humming along quietly, utilizing less than 5% of its CPU capacity, just serving up SMB file shares and running a couple of light containers.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Instead of letting cycles go to waste on an underutilized storage box or waking up a power-hungry desktop for background chores, you can shift constant workloads like media encoding, local LLMs, sync jobs, and scheduled indexing directly to the NAS. Your NAS isn't just a digital filing cabinet. It's a low-power, always-on compute node waiting to absorb the background operational burden from your main desktop.

I tried running everything off my NAS and realized where to draw the line

Your NAS can hit its limits if you host everything on it with reckless abandon

3
By  Ayush Pande

Your desktop is too power-hungry already

Give it some time off

Offloading desktop tasks makes a lot of technical and financial sense. When you run background tasks on a desktop, it can lead to a major power penalty. Leaving a dedicated desktop workstation running overnight or keeping it awake for local cron jobs, torrent seeding, or file conversions can incur a massive electric penalty due to dedicated GPUs, chipset power draw, and high idle motherboards. Your desktop is likely to draw tens if not up to hundreds of watts more than a NAS system would. While it might only be a small amount of electricity at a time, over a year you could waste hundreds of dollars.

In comparison, modern NAS or home server builds, even if they're mid-range Intel or efficient mini PC builds, can feature multicore processors with massive burst capacity. Even with this, they have low idle power states (C-states), meaning absorbing light to moderate background tasks barely registers on your power bill. You're only using the idle CPU headroom left on your already-running device.

There are a range of chores you can migrate

Move all of these tasks away from your desktop

It's important to know exactly what processes to move off of your desktop. There are some specific workloads that pretty much belong on a 24/7 NAS instead of a daily driver PC.

The first is automated media post-processing and transcoding. You can move Handbrake usage, TDArr optimization nodes, or Plex/Jellyfin metadata refreshing away from your primary desktop. That way you can game, work, and use your PC without stuttering and also don't have to leave it on in the background while these processes are happening.

The second process you may benefit from migrating is local data syncing and cloud backups. You can shift your Nextcloud sync loops, rsync off-site backup targets, and torrent/download management (like QBit Torrent Plus ARR stack) straight to the NAS storage arrays where the data lives natively anyway.

Any lightweight containerized utilities run smoothly on a low-powered NAS anyway, so you can run applications like Pi-hole, Uptime Kuma, Home Assistant integrations, or local AI helper containers on the server (instead of spinning up virtual machines on your primary work machine whenever you need them).

One thing to keep in mind is your NAS system's CPU power. Make sure you have enough compute cycles to complete all these tasks and open applications before you migrate them from your desktop.

How to move your chores over

Keep track of your CPU

If you're ready to put your spare NAS cycles to work, then here is an offloading blueprint.

Start by auditing your current system load. Use monitoring tools to measure what your NAS CPU is actually doing during peak and off-peak hours. That way, you can understand how much extra compute you have left to use. There are external tools like Grafana or Prometheus. However, a lot of NAS systems come with built-in simple `top`/`htop` utilities so that you have all of the information.

The next step is to containerize the chores. You can migrate background applications, like download clients, media processors, and sync tools, into isolated Docker containers on the NAS to keep resource boundaries strict. Make sure you set resource caps using Docker CPU and memory limit flags so background scripts never starve your primary storage services and cause out-of-memory panics. While many of these processes and applications use very little CPU, running them all at once can easily clog your NAS.

And with that, you're ready to power down your desktop at the end of the day with total peace of mind (knowing that your automated stack is handling business quietly in the background rather than you needing to leave on a very expensive and power-hungry desktop overnight).

You're leaving compute cycles to go to waste

Take advantage of your idle NAS

Most home servers are drastically underspec'd in terms of actual utilization compared to their physical capabilities. Shifting background chores from your primary desktop to your idle NAS is a win-win for energy bills, hardware longevity, and peace of mind in your daily workflow. Stop letting your storage server sit around doing half measures. Audit your daily desktop chores, containerize them, and you can let your NAS earn its keep 24/7.

item.title: Your “high performance” power plan might be hurting your CPU's gaming performance
item.itunes:title: Your “high performance” power plan might be hurting your CPU's gaming performance
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
After a fresh Windows install, PC gamers will immediately rush to the power settings to switch on the "high performance" power plan, which, if nothing else, is harmless. It does what it says on the tin, favoring the highest performance possible in exchange for higher energy usage. The advice has circulated on forums for over a decade, and while for most systems it definitely doesn't hurt to turn on, Ryzen dual-CCD CPUs specifically can actually have their performance hampered by doing so.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
AMD doesn't care about Intel anymore — the Ryzen 9 9950X3D just wins

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D is the best of both worlds, offering chart-topping performance in both gaming and productivity.

5
By  Jacob Roach

Dual-CCD X3D chips need the default setting

Balanced is the way to go to keep games on the right cores

AMD’s dual-CCD X3D processors—the 7900X3D, 7950X3D, 9900X3D, and 9950X3D—split their cores across two chiplets. Only one of them carries the stacked 3D V-Cache that makes these specific chips so strong in games. The other chiplet clocks higher, but has far less L3 cache, so for most games, you want every thread on the cache die because moving between chiplets adds via the Infinity Fabric adds latency.

The processor itself can't tell whether a program is a game, so AMD relies on Windows to do so. The chipset driver uses Game Bar's game detection as the signal to park the cores on the higher frequency chiplet, and with those cores parked, Windows schedules the game on the die with the 3D V-Cache

This is where power plans come into play. AMD recommends keeping systems running a dual-CCD CPU on the "Balanced" power plan, and there's good reason behind that. Owners who kept the High performance habit have reported that core parking doesn’t engage until they switch back, which could cause Windows to schedule the game across both chiplets instead of just the one with the extra cache. The extra latency of having to communicate across the chiplets can cause some significant performance loss.

AMD's X3D CPUs only help with two things, and most gamers have neither

3D V-Cache isn't a reason to buy blindly.

11
By  Hamlin Rozario

Modern CPUs don't need Windows to hold their clocks up

They can handle that on their own

Even outside the X3D case, the original reason for High performance has largely disappeared. The plan’s defining traits are that it pins the minimum processor state at 100%, stops cores from parking, and makes Windows quicker to raise clocks, and all of this mattered when the operating system managed CPU frequency directly and a frequency change could take around 30 milliseconds. Holding clocks high was a blunt but pretty effective way to avoid that lag. The thing is: modern CPUs don't need this.

Intel’s Speed Shift, introduced with Skylake, hands frequency control to the CPU and cuts transitions to roughly a millisecond. On the Red Team side of things, CPPC2 arrived for Ryzen in Summer 2019. AMD said it brought clock ramp times down from about 30 ms to 1 to 2 ms, and at that speed, there’s little left for a power plan to fix. Once a game is running, the cores it uses are already boosting. High performance mostly changes what happens when you aren’t gaming: the CPU idles hotter and draws more power, and the fans respond accordingly.

Here's exactly why AMD's X3D CPUs are better than Intel's for gaming

If you want a new gaming CPU, there are really only a few options you should consider.

6
By  Adam Conway

High performance power plans still have a use

And that's why they still exist

If it was totally pointless, the high performance power plan probably wouldn't exist anymore, but some hardware can still leave performance on the table on the Balanced plan. On Intel's hybrid processors like the Alder Lake chips, Windows decides which work goes to P-cores and which goes to E-cores, and the power plan influences that through its scheduling policy. Developer Alois Kraus found that on Windows 10, Balanced’s default policy could push lower-priority work onto E-cores. High performance’s policy favors the faster cores, which would matter for games.

5 reasons high-end CPUs have become overkill in 2025

Most users don't need to buy more than 8 cores

28
By  Tanveer Singh

Balanced should be the choice for most people

Even if you're chasing frames

In his investigation, Kraus found that the same effect was far less dramatic on Windows 11, and that's probably due to Intel's Thread Director giving hints as to which cores suit which threads. You also don’t necessarily need the high performance plan to achieve its behavior. Some X3D owners have duplicated the Balanced plan and edited it to mirror high performance, keeping core parking intact and seeing no benchmark difference. Reports conflict on this, though: Hardware Busters found that customizing the plan through the legacy Control Panel broke core parking on its 9950X3D, so I'd just stick with Balanced for the time being.

5 reasons high-end CPUs have become overkill in 2025

Most users don't need to buy more than 8 cores

28
By  Tanveer Singh

Power plans are best left at their default settings

Setting your Windows power plan to High performance isn't dangerous, but the one-size-fits-all advice of setting it and forgetting it simply isn't applicable anymore. For most CPUs it is harmless for performance, but for some it's actually detrimental. If you own a dual-CCD X3D chip, check your power plan today. For everyone else, switching back to Balanced will most likely make no difference in games and give you a cooler, quieter idle.

High performance mostly changes what happens when you aren’t gaming: the CPU idles hotter and draws more power, and the fans respond accordingly.

High performance power plans still have a use

And that's why they still exist

High performance’s policy favors the faster cores, which would matter for games.

Most users don't need to buy more than 8 cores

28
By  Tanveer Singh

Balanced should be the choice for most people

Even if you're chasing frames

In his investigation, Kraus found that the same effect was far less dramatic on Windows 11, and that's probably due to Intel's Thread Director giving hints as to which cores suit which threads. You also don’t necessarily need the high performance plan to achieve its behavior. Most users don't need to buy more than 8 cores

28
By  Tanveer Singh

Power plans are best left at their default settings

Setting your Windows power plan to High performance isn't dangerous, but the one-size-fits-all advice of setting it and forgetting it simply isn't applicable anymore. For most CPUs it is harmless for performance, but for some it's actually detrimental. If you own a dual-CCD X3D chip, check your power plan today. For everyone else, switching back to Balanced will most likely make no difference in games and give you a cooler, quieter idle.

item.title: Docker runs containers with root privileges by default, and that's a bigger risk than most people realize
item.itunes:title: Docker runs containers with root privileges by default, and that's a bigger risk than most people realize
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Although LXCs and Podman have their own perks, Docker remains the most popular container runtime for home labbers, and for good reason. Typical FOSS tools tend to ship with Docker images that work right out-of-the-box, with Compose configs simplifying the deployment process even further. Combine that with the ultra-simple Docker management commands, and it’s pretty easy to tinker with this runtime, even when you’re a complete beginner to containerized services.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That said, Docker has its own set of quirks. Its Swarm functionality isn’t as powerful as Kubernetes, while its daemon service can hog more resources compared to the daemonless architecture of certain rivals. However, my biggest issue with Docker is that it runs with root-level access by default, which is one heck of a security nightmare if you’re as fond of experimenting with random GitHub repos as I am.

NixOS containers are pretty exciting, and here's why I like them more than Docker

NixOS' containerization utility is far from perfect, but it's yet another aspect I love about the distro

3
By  Ayush Pande

A fresh Docker installation runs the daemon process (and containers) with root privileges

This increases the blast radius of vulnerable containers

If you’ve ever worked with Linux distributions, you’re probably aware that your setup has an admin account with unrestricted system access called root. When you install Docker for the first time, the underlying daemon process, dockerd, binds itself to the Unix socket owned by this root user. Unless you tweak certain parameters in a container’s Dockerfile, the environments spawned from dockerd also run with root privileges, and that’s where things get hairy from a security standpoint.

Unlike virtual machines, which emulate a fresh kernel and OS, containers share the kernel with the underlying host machine. Combine that with the fact that the dockerd daemon has full-on root-level access to the system, and Docker’s rootful design becomes a massive security nightmare. Let’s say a container image has some malicious code tacked on in a recent update. On a default Docker setup, it’d be a lot easier for this malicious code to escape its containerized confines and wreak havoc on your host machine.

Heck, it’s not just malware-riddled container images that you need to watch out for, either. If you accidentally mount a system directory to a container, your FOSS service will gain full-on superuser access to the critical files in this folder. And one botched container experiment is all it’d take to render the underlying host inaccessible.

Docker vs. Podman: Which one's better for your self-hosting needs?

Can Podman dethrone Docker to become the king of containerization platforms?

By  Ayush Pande

I stick to rootless Docker setups on my self-hosting workstations

It’s also fairly easy to enable

Technically, there are a couple of ways to make your Docker experiments more secure. You could modify the Dockerfile to force the container to run with non-root privileges. Or, for folks who use pre-built Docker images, you could override the user manually in the docker run or compose.yml files. But since both methods require you to repeat the same steps for every Docker container, this process can get tedious before long.

Instead, I recommend going down the rootless mode route, which also tackles the problem of the dockerd daemon running with superuser privileges. Since the container and the daemon remain locked behind an unprivileged user, a malfunctioning Docker environment can’t get full-on root access to the host machine with this mode. Better yet, you can just enable it once by running the following commands and have every new Docker container run with rootless permissions:

sudo apt install uidmap -y
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com/rootless | sh
export PATH=/usr/bin:$PATH
export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/1000/docker.sock

That said, rootless mode has its own set of caveats

Personally, I stick with rootless containers on my Docker workstations, and most of the services in my FOSS arsenal work well without any issues. However, running Docker environments with non-root privileges can introduce some minor issues. For one, you can’t map privileged ports for containers on a rootless Docker setup, meaning any ports under 1024 are off-limits for your containerized environments. It’s not a big deal for typical productivity apps, archival utilities, or backup services, but network tools are a different story altogether.

Take Pi-hole, for example, which needs access to port 53 for core DNS services. Of course, you can still deploy it on a rootless setup by tweaking certain config files, but it’s not as easy as executing a docker run command on a default Docker configuration. Besides the networking aspect, you’ll also need to deal with certain storage constraints, especially if your experiments involve OverlayFS mounts. Likewise, limiting resources for containers via cgroups v2 can be a bit of a hassle, and the same holds true for custom AppArmor profiles.

But for folks looking to tinker with productivity tools, quirky container images, and data archival utilities, it’s a good idea to enable rootless mode on Docker.

item.itunes:title: My Raspberry Pi Zero is too slow for anything general, but it's perfect for one specific job
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is a small upgrade over its predecessor, with no focus on memory or processor improvements. It's a great device for learning the ropes, interacting with an SBC via CLI or SSH, and even running a few lightweight containers. Yet compared with boards like the Raspberry Pi 5 or the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, it doesn't seem appealing at all. My first SBC was a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and I went on to buy one more because it made sense for a different purpose.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After spending years with the board and optimizing every bit of it for maximum power, I find it useful for niche projects. Although it's the least-preferred board in the Raspberry Pi lineup, it runs Pi-hole and saves me from tracking, ads, and public DNS logging. Let's explore how I built it and the method to improve it.

Pi-hole is a free, low-demand DNS sinkhole

Pairing it with Unbound increases your privacy

Like any other SBC or mini server, installing Pi-hole is straightforward. But I don't use direct package installations and prefer Docker. It reduces dependency conflicts, is easy to maintain once you learn it, and makes troubleshooting easier. If the containers misbehave, you can still access your server and troubleshoot the problem.

A Pi-hole installation creates a DNS sinkhole and intercepts DNS requests from your home devices. It uses a blocklist, or multiple lists if needed, to block most ads and tracking strategies websites use. The result is a cleaner, privacy-focused web surfing experience across multiple devices. But your DNS queries still go through a public DNS provider like Google or Cloudflare.

Encrypting DNS queries through Pi-hole is where the real privacy happens, and it only took 10 minutes

It made my network security so much better

By  Charles Wolfe

Unbound can offer a more secure recursive DNS experience. It leaves ads and tracking to Pi-hole and handles DNS resolution. So, your DNS requests don't go through a public DNS provider. Unbound uses authoritative DNS servers to handle this job. Most users deploy Pi-hole and ignore this crucial aspect.

Building the DNS duo

Docker, lean SBC OS, and Tailscale

How do you make all these components work on a Raspberry Pi with just 512MB of memory? You start with a lean operating system. The OS should be lightweight, well-supported, and make SBC interaction consistent. DietPi ticks all these checkboxes and is my favorite pick, even on x86 systems. It uses about 70MB of memory on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, which is the lowest usage so far. There's no gimmick behind it, and the built-in CLI tools are the icing on the cake. The interface stays similar even when you SSH in, which makes it a joy to experiment with.

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W reserves some memory for GPU rendering, leaving only 410MB for your setup. Docker needs an additional 50MB, which still leaves plenty for Pi-hole and Unbound. I have tried installing Pi-hole directly before, but I eventually preferred Docker. After a quick Unbound configuration and the deployment of Pi-hole and Unbound containers, the setup was ready to work.

5 incredibly useful services you can self-host on a single Raspberry Pi

For such a tiny single-board computer, there's a lot of potential for your home lab in those chips

3
By  Jeff Butts

If you want your Raspberry Pi to handle DNS queries, you'll also need to change your router settings. My Tenda router isn't advanced and has DHCP enabled. So, I only had to change the ISP DNS address to the Raspberry Pi's DNS address, and that worked. Now, all devices send requests to the router, which then forwards them to my custom DNS server powered by Unbound and Pi-hole.

Even after all this, the SBC has 40 percent idle memory, which means fewer crashes. You can take an additional measure and install Tailscale on the SBC to make it accessible outside the Tailscale network. You can also make all your Tailnet devices use the Pi-hole, but I didn't implement it. If something goes wrong with Pi-hole, new DNS requests won't go through.

There’s also a concern about a fallback DNS server if your Pi-hole setup fails due to technical reasons like a crash, device failure, or data corruption. You have two ways to fix it. The first one is pretty simple: use a public DNS provider, but that defeats the point of using this setup. Or you could set up another Pi-hole and Unbound. Since there is no guarantee which one the router will use, having a public DNS server will turn off the ad-blocking, privacy-focused experience you want.

Post-deployment measures

A self-healing script

Ideally, this setup should run without manual intervention until there’s a problem with Docker or the SBC itself. But when it happens and if you don’t have an alternate DNS server mentioned in the router settings, you suddenly cannot access new websites. It’s not your router's fault; you told it to use the Pi-hole setup, which isn't working now. Most of the time it's a glitched service or Docker antics, and SSHing to the SBC and then running troubleshooting commands is a pain.

I use a self-healing script that does all the routine troubleshooting tasks for me. It runs in the background with a timer and tries to sort the problem intelligently. The script checks whether Pi-hole is running and whether Unbound can resolve queries. It’s much more granular than Docker’s internal checks and also tests the internet connection.

My Raspberry Pi now fixes itself when services die, and I haven't SSHed in weeks

My custom script monitors Docker, Pi‑Hole, Unbound and Tailscale

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

The script performs a reboot only when multiple checks fail, and it’s designed that way. Rather than using reboot as a regular troubleshooting method, it reserves it for long-standing problems. Without this script, it'd be just an impending disaster that would break the internet connection for nearly a dozen devices.

My personal DNS server

A Raspberry Pi Zero is a weak SBC that is now a central point of my home network. DNS requests go through it, and I get an ad-free experience without paying a dime. While the board is hard to find these days, I highly recommend it as a Pi-hole device if you have one lying around collecting dust.

Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is a small upgrade over its predecessor, with no focus on memory or processor improvements. It's a great device for learning the ropes, interacting with an SBC via CLI or SSH, and even running a few lightweight containers. Yet compared with boards like the Raspberry Pi 5 or the Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, it doesn't seem appealing at all. My first SBC was a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and I went on to buy one more because it made sense for a different purpose.

After spending years with the board and optimizing every bit of it for maximum power, I find it useful for niche projects. Although it's the least-preferred board in the Raspberry Pi lineup, it runs Pi-hole and saves me from tracking, ads, and public DNS logging. Let's explore how I built it and the method to improve it.

Pi-hole is a free, low-demand DNS sinkhole

Pairing it with Unbound increases your privacy

Like any other SBC or mini server, installing Pi-hole is straightforward. But I don't use direct package installations and prefer Docker. It reduces dependency conflicts, is easy to maintain once you learn it, and makes troubleshooting easier. If the containers misbehave, you can still access your server and troubleshoot the problem.

A Pi-hole installation creates a DNS sinkhole and intercepts DNS requests from your home devices. It uses a blocklist, or multiple lists if needed, to block most ads and tracking strategies websites use. The result is a cleaner, privacy-focused web surfing experience across multiple devices. But your DNS queries still go through a public DNS provider like Google or Cloudflare.

Encrypting DNS queries through Pi-hole is where the real privacy happens, and it only took 10 minutes

It made my network security so much better

By  Charles Wolfe

Unbound can offer a more secure recursive DNS experience. It leaves ads and tracking to Pi-hole and handles DNS resolution. So, your DNS requests don't go through a public DNS provider. Unbound uses authoritative DNS servers to handle this job. Most users deploy Pi-hole and ignore this crucial aspect.

Building the DNS duo

Docker, lean SBC OS, and Tailscale

How do you make all these components work on a Raspberry Pi with just 512MB of memory? You start with a lean operating system. The OS should be lightweight, well-supported, and make SBC interaction consistent. DietPi ticks all these checkboxes and is my favorite pick, even on x86 systems. It uses about 70MB of memory on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, which is the lowest usage so far. There's no gimmick behind it, and the built-in CLI tools are the icing on the cake. The interface stays similar even when you SSH in, which makes it a joy to experiment with.

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W reserves some memory for GPU rendering, leaving only 410MB for your setup. Docker needs an additional 50MB, which still leaves plenty for Pi-hole and Unbound. I have tried installing Pi-hole directly before, but I eventually preferred Docker. After a quick Unbound configuration and the deployment of Pi-hole and Unbound containers, the setup was ready to work.

For such a tiny single-board computer, there's a lot of potential for your home lab in those chips

item.itunes:summary:
Buying a bargain projector is an attractive proposition that crumbles long before your movie night begins, and you end up pixel-peeping or lamenting the image quality.

When I first shopped for a compact projector that I could move around the house and aim at my wall for a 90-inch screen, I bought a moderately sized, white-labeled Chinese projector with a native 720p resolution for under $400. While I expected softer details from a budget 720p panel, I never anticipated how much daily friction the surrounding hardware and software shortcuts would create every time I repositioned the unit or operated it.

Two maddening flaws finally pushed me over the edge: a cooling fan that screamed like a helicopter at liftoff, and unreliable firmware missing quality-of-life essentials you'd expect on a projector. Moreover, I didn't even know about these limitations until I upgraded to the XGIMI Horizon S Max last year. It occupies a slightly larger footprint but transforms the day-to-day experience of portable home projection. Living with both machines side by side exposes six issues you're better off knowing before you face them.

1 Cheap cooling systems

Stealing the silence from your quiet scenes

A projector that whines like a hair dryer destroys the tension of a thriller or a late-night drama within minutes of pressing play. Because I constantly move my projector around the room instead of bolting it to the ceiling, the chassis usually sits on a table right beside or behind my seating area. My sub-$400 projector ramped its fan up to a shrill whine reminiscent of laptops running CineBench. If I didn't have ANC buds in, or the volume turned up enough, I often lost the cinematic brilliance of quiet scenes to this sound that ultimately forced me to replace the projector.

Budget manufacturers create this acoustic nightmare when they cram hot LED arrays into poorly ventilated plastic shells, smear bargain thermal paste across undersized heatsinks, and install tiny fans that immediately hit max speed so loudly the cheap speakers cannot mask their roar.

Proper thermal design that accounts for heat generation with adequate ventilation cutouts and internal air ducting would easily solve this fan noise problem. The XGIMI Horizon S Max moves heat through a well-ventilated chassis that keeps fan noise at or below 28dB during standard viewing modes, letting me place the projector right next to my couch and hear whispered dialogue from the film instead.

This projector gives me a 120-inch 4K screen for gaming that's cheaper than most high-end monitors

Gaming in 4K60 for that superior immersion.

By  Chandraveer Mathur

2 Poor firmware choices

Missing Widevine DRM makes streaming a chore

Pathetic, half-baked software running on underpowered hardware turns simple tasks like opening an app into a routine headache you cannot bypass without additional expense on a streaming stick. My sub-$400 unit ran an outdated, uncertified fork of Android on an underpowered chipset that delayed every remote click by a second.

Worse, the firmware lacked Widevine L1 DRM certification — restricting Prime Video and Netflix to blurry standard definition — and offered no firmware recovery options when a buggy system update froze the launcher. Sure, the native 720p resolution didn't need Widevine L1, and XGIMI's official Netflix Installation guide openly notes that the Horizon S Max lacks native Netflix certification, but the latter redeems the everyday software experience through a snappy Android TV 11.0 interface.

A smart projector is self-sufficient on the software front only if the manufacturer pairs capable hardware with stable system support and the certification needed to stream media in the best supported resolution. Xgimi backs its experience with dependable firmware and built-in recovery options. Moreover, its HDMI 2.1 port includes full HDMI CEC support, so I plug in a dedicated streaming stick and control my entire media library smoothly using a single remote.

3 Manual keystone adjustments

Waste time every time you move the projector

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

For anyone who moves a projector around the house or takes it camping, missing or manual-only keystone correction steals ten minutes of setup time before every use. Whenever I placed my budget 720p projector on a table at a slight angle to the wall, I had to wedge books under the plastic feet and use the laggy remote to drag four distorted corners projected on the wall into something resembling a rectangle. The model I bought had vertical keystone, but not horizontal, and its small size meant even slight placement adjustments while tidying up the room forced manual keystone all over again.

Modern spatial sensors and mechanical mounts turn that tedious alignment chore into an invisible two-second step. The XGIMI Horizon S Max integrates a 360-degree horizontal and 135-degree vertical gimbal stand into the body, so books for tilt and off-center projection become non-issues.

Pair that with a TOF sensor, and you get uninterrupted, motion-sensing, and automatic keystone plus autofocus. Sure, we're still getting digital zoom for obstacle avoidance, but that four-way automatic keystone is a massive convenience upgrade. Now I just set the unit down anywhere, point it at a wall or screen, and it does the rest.

4 Dust kills your projectors

The cheaper ones skip on protections and die faster

Exposing a projector to even household dust shortens its lifespan, making a missing lens cap and an unsealed light engine some very serious shortfalls. Most cheap projectors lack them, exposing the front lens element to dust and potentially abrasive particles that can erode coatings when wiped off. Lest I forget, there's always the off chance of fingerprints or damage from improper handling. Cheap devices pull ambient air straight across the internal lens stack, baking dark dust blobs into the light path that show up as spots you cannot wipe away.

Cleaning internal dust out of an unsealed budget projector typically requires professional intervention, and the Horizon S Max removes both risks with a sealed DLP optical engine that keeps dust out, and a motorized woolen-fabric sliding cover for the front element.

I ditched my monitor for a 4K 120Hz projector, and it completely changed my setup

Swapping my monitor for a 4K 120Hz projector gave me a bigger screen and a home theater.

1
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Spec sheets hide the daily friction

Living with a cheap projector taught me that resolution, refresh rate, and lamp brightness mean little when your experience is marred by screaming fans, tinny speakers that cannot mask them, keystone that lasts through the movie's opening sequence, horrible software and firmware adding insult to injury, and dust buildup if you somehow put up with all that precedes it.

Upgrading to a premium projector gets you necessities often mistaken for creature comforts, or you'll default to a large TV next time and save everyone the hassle.

item.title: I changed one channel width setting on my Wi-Fi 6 router, and local streaming stutter completely stopped
item.itunes:title: I changed one channel width setting on my Wi-Fi 6 router, and local streaming stutter completely stopped
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Sometimes, even when you're streaming a high-bitrate 4K Blu-ray remux or a heavy game stream from a local server like Plex or a PC VR setup, you might still encounter random micro-stutters, frame drops, and audio sync issues despite having a modern Wi-Fi 6 router. You'll easily troubleshoot everything before you can determine the actual root cause: the invisible bottleneck sitting in the router is a wireless configuration.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Most Wi-Fi 6 routers ship out of the box with conservative 5GHz channel-width settings, typically locked to 80MHz to ensure broad compatibility, leaving massive performance headroom untapped (or, conversely, struggling with a narrow slice of spectrum). By digging into your router's wireless settings and aligning your 5GHz channel width configuration, you can double your theoretical link rate, clear out packet queuing delays, and completely eliminate local streaming stutter.

Your neighbors' Wi-Fi is slowing yours down, and one simple setting can fix it

Your router's default wireless channel may not be the most optimal

4
By  Tanveer Singh

Your channel width settings can impact your LAN

How does channel width actually work?

To understand why these settings matter, you need to know what channel width means for local data throughput. It doesn't just impact your internet connection; it can impact your LAN connection too.

If you think of channel width like lanes on a highway, a standard 20MHz or 40MHz channel is a narrow road, whereas an 80MHz channel is a standard multi-lane highway. A 160MHz channel, or even a well-managed 80MHz block, acts like a wide-open superhighway. When you see it that way, it makes sense to choose those wider channels so you can let more through.

For example, doubling your channel width from 80MHz to 160MHz doubles your physical-layer link rate, jumping from 1,200Mbps to 2,400Mbps on a 2x2 Wi-Fi 6 client. However, it also widens your receiver's net, making it more vulnerable to neighborhood interference and raising the noise floor if not tuned correctly. That's something that you have to keep in mind. Your throughput will go up, but you'll trade off against interference, especially in congested areas like apartment buildings or busy suburbs.

How to fix your channel width settings

It's a simple adjustment

High-bitrate local streaming can choke on default settings. Default router configurations fail these heavy local workloads because a true 4K HDR Blu-ray remux can spike past 80 to sometimes even 100+Mbps during intense action sequences. When background interference causes micro packet drops on a restricted channel width, the TCP retransmissions cause immediate buffering and playback stutter.

There's a big danger with over-congested frequencies. If your router's auto channel selection forces you into a crowded lower band spectrum using wide channels, co-channel interference from neighboring networks will tank your frame pacing (even if your raw signal bars look full).

If you want to fix your wireless stutter, start by auditing your RF environment. You can use a Wi-Fi analyzer tool on your mobile phone to check which 5GHz channels are the least congested in your home. I find the best way to do this is to move around my house and take readings from different areas of my home. That way, I can see where interference is worst and where there might be a safer area.

Once you have this information, you can access your advanced wireless settings by logging into your router's administrative dashboard and going to the 5GHz wireless radio configuration page. Here you should find settings to adjust the channel width. You can toggle your 5GHz channel width from the default setting, which is usually stuck on auto or 80MHz (sometimes even lower), to 160MHz if your environment and hardware support it, or you can lock down a clean, non-overlapping 80MHz block paired with a clear channel.

Once you've done this, it's time to test and verify that it works. You can use a Wi-Fi analyzer tool again to see if anything has changed and also fire up a high-bitrate 4K RMX on a local stream and monitor your frame pacing and throughput metrics to ensure stutter is entirely gone.

Keep the practical hurdles in mind

There may be some instances where wider isn't better

As I mentioned earlier, there are hurdles with 160MHz, and one of the biggest is the apartment complex trap. By enabling 160MHz in a dense urban environment where every neighbor has a Wi-Fi 6 router, this can backfire on you immensely.

Use a Wi-Fi analyzer to see which spectrums are overlapping. If you choose a heavily overlapping spectrum, then you can turn your brand-new wide highway into gridlock traffic. A better option, if you are in this environment and do have neighbors' signals interfering in your home, is choosing a clean non-overlapping 80 MHz block paired with that clear channel. A smaller, empty road is better than a bigger road covered in traffic.

Another thing to consider is ensuring client device compatibility. Make sure all your streaming clients, whether they're high-end laptops, a dedicated media box, or a wireless VR headset, support that wide channel bonding. The majority of modern devices do, but some legacy devices don't.

Don't stick to the default settings

Make your router work for you

Manufacturers ship routers with safe, conservative defaults that leave half your wireless performance on the table. Adjusting a single channel width setting can transform your network from an inconsistent bottleneck into a blazing-fast local streaming pipeline. Stop accepting micro-stuttering during movie night. Log in to your router's advanced settings and give your local streams the bandwidth highway that they were built for.
